text:
Oh, I'm so glad you asked. Most people never consider the matter, which is precisely why the world is drowning in damp hands and bacterial aerosols.

Hand dryers are, quite simply, an affront to hygiene, acoustics, and common sense.

First, the conventional warm-air dryer. It takes roughly forty-five seconds to dry one's hands, during which time most people give up and wipe the residual moisture on their trousers. So now you have a damp, bacteria-friendly patch on your pants, which, I might add, is exactly where you don't want one.

Then there's the jet-style dryer, the kind you plunge your hands into like a hot dog into a bun. Those blast air at hundreds of miles per hour, which sounds efficient until you realize what they're doing: launching microscopic droplets of water, and whatever was living in that water, all over the restroom. Studies have found that these devices can spread viral particles considerably farther than paper towels do. Essentially, you are standing inside a germ cannon. Some people call that drying. I call it biological warfare with a chrome finish.

And don't get me started on the noise. Many of them exceed ninety decibels. That is comparable to a lawnmower. I go to the restroom for relief, not to be sonically assaulted.

Paper towels, by contrast, physically remove bacteria through friction, dry hands quickly, and can be used to open the door handle on your way out. That last point is crucial, because the door handle has been touched by every person who didn't wash their hands at all. And statistically, that's a lot of people. I've counted.

Now, some will argue that hand dryers are more environmentally friendly. Fine. I care about the planet. But I also care about not contracting norovirus from a stranger's fingertips. When I must use a restroom with only a hand dryer, I carry my own paper towels. And hand sanitizer. And, on one occasion, a small battery-operated fan, but Leonard said that made people uncomfortable.

So, my verdict: hand dryers are loud, slow, unsanitary, and a monument to humanity's willingness to accept mediocrity in the name of saving a few trees.

Bazinga? No. I'm entirely serious.
